title: What was running on this computer? A first look at a RAM dump
short: First look at a RAM dump
lead: Memory holds what a disk does not: running programs, open network connections and code that never touched a file. This workflow is a first pass over a Windows memory dump with Volatility 3.
evidence: A memory (RAM) dump of a Windows computer
answers: Which programs were running when memory was captured
What command line each program was started with
Which processes deserve a closer look
need: A memory dump file, or a practice dump (see the practice section on this page)
An internet connection on first use, so that Volatility can fetch the Windows symbol files it needs

steps.title: Capture memory first, if the computer is still on
steps.text: Memory is lost when the computer is switched off, so capture it before anything else. Run the capture tool from a USB drive and save the dump to that drive, not to the computer's own disk. Note the time and the tool used.
steps.note: Running a capture tool changes a small part of memory. That is accepted practice, but write down that you did it.

steps.title: Check that Volatility can read the dump
steps.text: Run the info plugin. If it prints the Windows version and system time, the dump is readable and you can continue. Note the system time: it is when the dump was taken.

steps.title: List the processes
steps.text: pslist shows the processes Windows itself was tracking. pstree shows the same list as a tree, so you can see which program started which. Look for odd names, odd parents (for example a document program starting a command shell) and programs running from temporary folders.

steps.title: Look for hidden or finished processes
steps.text: psscan searches memory for process records directly. A process that psscan finds and pslist does not may have ended already, or may have been hidden. Compare the two lists.

steps.title: Read the command lines
steps.text: cmdline shows how each process was started, including any options and file names passed to it. This often explains what a suspicious process was doing.

steps.title: List network connections
steps.text: netscan lists connections and listening ports, with the process that owned each one. Note any unexpected remote addresses for the processes you flagged.

steps.title: Flag possible injected code
steps.text: malfind points out memory regions that look like code placed inside another process. Its results are leads, not findings: normal software triggers it too. Follow up only on the processes you already had doubts about.

steps.title: Browse and cross-check
steps.text: MemProcFS shows the same dump as folders and files, which makes it easy to browse a process and confirm what Volatility reported. Record the tool versions, the commands you ran and the dump's hash value.

artifacts.name: windows.info
artifacts.tells: Windows version and the time of the dump

artifacts.name: windows.pslist / pstree
artifacts.tells: Processes Windows was tracking, and their parents

artifacts.name: windows.psscan
artifacts.tells: Process records found by scanning, including ended or hidden ones

artifacts.name: windows.netscan
artifacts.tells: Connections and listening ports, with the owning process

artifacts.name: windows.malfind
artifacts.tells: Memory regions that may hold injected code (leads only)

limits: A memory dump shows one moment. It does not show what happened before, except for traces that happened to remain.
Memory changes while it is being captured, so some records can be inconsistent.
malfind and similar plugins produce false alarms. A flagged process is not proof of malware.
If the computer was switched off before capture, live memory is gone. A hibernation file or page file on the disk may hold part of it.
Volatility needs symbol files that match the Windows build. Without them, plugins fail.
Plugin names and options change between Volatility versions. Check the documentation for the version you install.

practice.name: MemLabs
practice.text: A set of free practice labs for memory forensics in a capture-the-flag style, each with a memory dump to download and a short scenario.
practice.task: Download the first lab and run steps 2 to 6 of this workflow on its dump. Write down the Windows version, the processes that look out of place and the command lines they were started with.
